client: I've been having a really hard time since my brother passed away six months ago. Every time my friends invite me out or there's some kind of gathering, I just feel this hollow emptiness instead of enjoying myself like I used to. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: I'm really glad you decided to give this a shot, and I want you to know that what you're carrying — this grief, this hollow feeling in moments that used to bring joy — makes complete sense after losing your brother. That emptiness you describe at gatherings isn't a sign that something is permanently broken in you; it's often grief's way of reminding us how much someone mattered. I'm curious — when you're in those social situations and that hollow feeling shows up, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in those moments?

client: Honestly, the main thing that goes through my head is that my brother should be there with me. Like, he was the one who made those kinds of gatherings actually fun, and now I'm just standing there thinking about how wrong it feels that everyone else is laughing and carrying on like nothing happened. And then I start feeling guilty, like I'm betraying him somehow by even trying to enjoy myself.
therapist: That guilt you're describing — the feeling that enjoying yourself somehow betrays your brother — is one of the most common and painful parts of grief, and it speaks to how deeply you loved him. But I'd gently invite you to consider: do you think your brother would have wanted his memory to be the thing that keeps you from ever feeling joy again? It might be worth exploring whether allowing yourself small moments of happiness could actually be a way of honoring him, rather than leaving him behind — what do you think he would say if he could see you struggling with this guilt?

client: I know logically that he would probably tell me to stop moping around and go have a good time, because that's just who he was. But knowing that in my head and actually feeling okay about laughing at a party are two completely different things, and I don't know how to get from one to the other. It almost feels too simple, like just thinking about what he'd want isn't going to suddenly lift this weight off me.
therapist: You're absolutely right, and I want to validate that — grief doesn't heal just because we logic our way through it, and it would feel dismissive to suggest otherwise. What you're describing is actually a really important insight: there's often a gap between what we *know* and what we *feel*, and bridging that gap takes time and small, gentle steps rather than one big mental shift. I'm wondering — when you imagine being at a gathering and feeling that hollow emptiness, is there any tiny moment, even a fleeting one, where you've noticed even a sliver of something other than pain?

client: There was this one moment a few weeks ago where my friend said something that reminded me of an inside joke my brother and I used to have, and for like half a second I almost smiled. But then I immediately felt that guilt crash back in, like I had no right to find anything funny, and it kind of ruined the rest of the night. So I guess those slivers exist, but they almost make it worse because of what follows them.
therapist: That half-second almost-smile is actually really significant — it tells us that your capacity for joy isn't gone, it's just being intercepted by that guilt before it can fully land. What's worth noticing is that the smile came *through* a memory of your brother, which suggests that joy and grief aren't necessarily opposites here — that moment connected you to him rather than erasing him. I'm curious whether, if we could somehow soften that guilt response, you think you might be able to let moments like that inside-joke memory become a way of *being* with your brother rather than a reminder that he's gone?

client: That framing actually makes some sense to me, like maybe that smile wasn't a betrayal but more like he was briefly there with me in that moment. But I honestly don't know how you "soften" a guilt response, because when it hits it's not like I have any control over it, it just floods in. I guess I'm skeptical that there's actually a way to change that, because I've been trying to just push through it for six months and it hasn't gotten any easier.
therapist: Your skepticism makes complete sense — six months of pushing through and still hurting is exhausting, and you deserve an honest answer rather than false reassurance. The key insight from CBT is that we don't try to fight or suppress that guilt when it floods in, but instead learn to gently *notice* it and create just a tiny bit of space between the feeling and what it's telling you — almost like observing it rather than being swallowed by it. It's a skill that develops slowly with practice, not willpower, so I'm wondering — in that moment after the almost-smile, if you could have paused and whispered to yourself "there he is," do you think that might have felt different than the guilt narrative that rushed in?

client: That phrase "there he is" actually hit me in a way I wasn't expecting, and I can see how it might feel different from the guilt just taking over. But I'm worried that in the actual moment, when I'm at a party and everything is loud and chaotic, I won't have the presence of mind to do something that gentle and intentional. It feels like the kind of thing that might work in a quiet therapy office but fall apart when real life is happening around me.
therapist: That's a really honest and practical concern, and it actually shows good self-awareness about how you function under stress — the last thing I'd want is for this to become another thing you feel like you're failing at when the moment gets away from you. The good news is that "there he is" doesn't have to be perfectly timed or graceful; even if the guilt floods in first and you only remember the phrase five minutes later in the bathroom, that still counts as practice and still starts to reshape the pattern over time. I'm wondering if it might help to try this in a smaller, lower-stakes moment first — like when you're alone and a memory of him surfaces — so it starts to feel a little more familiar before you're in the middle of a loud gathering?

client: Practicing it alone actually sounds more manageable than trying it in a crowd, and I think I could maybe do that. But I'm a little worried that when I'm alone and a memory hits, it's already when I feel the loneliness the hardest, so I don't know if that's going to make things better or just open up a bigger hole. I guess I'm asking whether this is supposed to feel worse before it feels better, because I'm not sure I have the bandwidth for more pain right now.
therapist: That's such an important question to ask, and I want to be honest with you — sometimes gently leaning into grief does stir up feelings that were being kept at arm's length, but the goal here isn't to flood yourself with pain, it's to take the smallest possible step that feels survivable. You get to be in control of the pace, and if a solo memory moment feels like too much right now, we can find an even gentler starting point that doesn't ask more of you than you have to give. I'm curious — when you imagine a quiet moment where a memory of your brother surfaces, is there anything that already helps you feel even slightly more grounded or safe, something small that's already in your life?

client: There's this one playlist my brother and I used to listen to together, and sometimes when I put it on it feels like the closest thing to having him nearby rather than just feeling his absence. But even that is hit or miss, sometimes it's comforting and other times it just destroys me and I end up worse off than before. I guess that's the most honest answer I have, even if it's not a very reliable safety net.
therapist: The fact that you have something like that playlist — something that can sometimes bring him *near* rather than just underscoring his absence — is genuinely meaningful, even if it's unpredictable right now. That inconsistency isn't a flaw in you or the approach; it's just what grief looks like at six months, where the same thing can land completely differently depending on the day, your energy, or what else you're carrying. I'm wondering if rather than using the playlist as a safety net you have to rely on, you might experiment with putting it on just for a minute or two in a moment when you're already feeling relatively okay — not to fix anything, just to practice being with him in a small, contained way — does that feel like something worth trying, or does even that feel like too much right now?

client: A minute or two when I'm already feeling relatively okay sounds doable, and I think the "not to fix anything" part actually takes some pressure off because usually I go into those moments hoping they'll make me feel better and then I'm disappointed when they don't. I guess my hesitation is that I'm not always sure I can tell when I'm "relatively okay" versus just numb, because lately those two things feel kind of the same to me. I don't want to accidentally stumble into a bad moment thinking I was in a safe one.
therapist: That distinction you're drawing between "relatively okay" and "numb" is really perceptive, and it tells me that part of what grief has done is make it harder to read your own internal signals — which makes sense when you've been in survival mode for six months. Rather than trying to perfectly gauge your emotional state beforehand, maybe the experiment is simpler: just notice how your body feels before you press play — is your breathing relatively steady, are you sitting somewhere you feel physically safe — and let that be "okay enough" rather than requiring emotional certainty. I'm curious, when you imagine a moment like that — steady breath, familiar space, no pressure to feel better — does that feel like something your body might actually recognize as safe, even if your emotions are harder to read right now?

client: Using my body as a checkpoint instead of trying to figure out my emotions actually feels more concrete, like something I might be able to do without overthinking it. I think my body probably does know the difference between steady and not steady, even when my head is all over the place. I'm still a little nervous about it, but I guess a minute of music with steady breathing in my own apartment isn't the scariest thing I could try.
therapist: That nervousness you're feeling alongside the willingness to try is actually a really healthy sign — it means you're taking this seriously rather than just going through the motions, and that matters. You've just mapped out something genuinely concrete: a minute of your shared playlist, in your own space, with steady breathing, no pressure to feel anything in particular — and if it starts to feel like too much, you can simply press pause and that's not failure, that's you taking care of yourself. I want to ask — after everything we've talked about today, what feels most different about how you're thinking about these moments with your brother's memory, compared to when you first sat down?
